critic:set-consistency.verdict: Nothing blocking from this lens. horn-backD fits the set better than today's frames in every tint, so it should replace them. The nearest turn frames are turn-<tint>-03 and turn-<tint>-02. They use the same camera position as the horn-back. The turntable is at 160° and 145°, against the horn-back's 155°, and the lens is 125 mm against 95 mm. Today's horn-back was clearly the odd one out in Fog, on every surface. In Dust, Acid and Ice it was odd on the wall edge seen end-on and on the grips. horn-backD brings these to within about ±3.5 L* of the front and ampA2, and inside the range set by turn-02 and turn-03. Ember, Poison, Haze and Smoke move 2.5 L* or less, and were never odd beyond the lighting gap below. No tint now stands out: the spread across tints of (horn-back minus turn-03) shrinks on every surface. No tint washes out: chroma rises or holds on every tinted surface. The render-block rule holds: all 8 fronts, all 192 turn frames, all 8 ampA2 and all 8 horn-backD frames are 32/16/32, with diffuse 6 from render.py's default. What still separates the horn-back from the set is not path depth. The shot keeps its FA123-era lighting: a light-grey world at 0.7, key, fill and wash lamps, and no cards. It also has no finish. As a result the cabinet's back and its lettering render 8-20 L* darker than turn-03 at the same angle. This was already true of today's frames, and the new render does not change it. Comparing the horn-back with the turn also showed a problem in the other views: the Dust and Ice fronts, and the turn frames that face the back, push 24-31 % of the cabinet's main face to the top of a colour channel.

findings.claim: Why the acrylic brightened, tint by tint, and why the new look is what real acrylic does. The pixels that moved are views down 20 mm edges and frames that act as light guides. Cycles counts each total internal reflection (TIR) as a glossy bounce. At 12/8/8 these paths were cut at the 8th TIR, so the glossy and total limits did it, not transmission 8. A cut path returns black. At 32/16/32 the light arrives, coloured by absorption (Beer–Lambert) over about 0.5 m of tint, and the new edge colours match that prediction. Faces with the white lining behind them only ever needed about 5 events, so they did not change.
findings.evidence: Geometry: the camera sees the back face at 50.7° and the side walls' rear edges at about 51-53°. All of the ray's deviation runs across the 20 mm thickness. Inside the acrylic (n 1.49) the ray travels 31-32° off the sheet and meets the faces at 58°, past the 42° critical angle. That gives one TIR about every 32 mm, so about 13 TIR along the 420 mm depth (path about 498 mm). Add 2 refractions at the edge (in and out), 2 more through the front panel, and 1 diffuse bounce at the paper: about 16-18 events. A face backed by lining needs only wall in, white batting, wall out: 4 refractions and 1 diffuse. Cycles kernel/integrator/path_state.h: a reflection (TIR included) increments glossy_bounce, a refraction increments transmission_bounce, and both count toward max_bounce. When a limit is reached, the path flag TERMINATE_AFTER_TRANSPARENT means only emission at the next hit counts. Inside the acrylic the next hit is another face, so the path returns 0. Predicted transmission over 498 mm (deep colour raised to d/radius) against the measured new strip centre (x205-212, y680-880, linear RGB): Fog (1,1,1) vs (0.48,0.48,0.44); Dust (0.49,0,0) vs (0.263,0.006,0); Acid (0.078,0.044,0) vs (0.083,0.065,0); Ice (0,0,0.24) vs (0,0.012,0.140); Ember R 1e-4 vs 0.013; Haze B 0.006 vs 0.032; Poison and Smoke about 0 vs ≤0.003. Strip L*, today -> depth: Fog 34.9->74.7, Dust 12.9->29.5, Acid 19.5->30.4, Ice 7.5->15.0, Ember 1.7->2.8, Haze 1.5->2.6, Poison 1.3->1.8, Smoke 0.3->0.4. That is the order of each tint's long-path transmission; Smoke's lining is also black. Real acrylic does the same. Light entering an edge is totally internally reflected 'until it reaches another edge' (Straight Dope; critical angle 41.8° for n≈1.5, Wikipedia). That is why sheet edges read deeper than faces: Perspex Vario says 'the colour is most vivid on the edge rather than the face', and Perspex's clear long-path grade quotes 91% long-path transmission. So a clear 20 mm edge in a white studio should look bright and silvery, just under the paper (new Fog 70-75 vs paper 94), not grey or black as in today's frame. Dust's edges going red is predicted by the material's own note ('red travels farthest'). The new Fog cabinet also matches turn-fog-04, rendered at the same depth: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-super-hot/f4a25b5c-7cd5-585d-b4f3-c7ba36b6c676/scratchpad/b105/real-clean/compare-turn04-hbD-fog.jpg.
